topic: ConfigMaps, Secrets, ServiceAccounts and security contexts

notes.front: What are Linux capabilities?
notes.back: Separate privileges that can be granted to a process without granting it all the privileges of the root user.
notes.explanation: In Kubernetes you add or drop them per container, in the `capabilities` field of the container's `securityContext`.
notes.example: Like giving a contractor the key to the server room only, instead of the master key to the whole building.
notes.evidence: With Linux capabilities, you can grant certain privileges to a process without granting all the privileges of the root user. To add or drop Linux capabilities for a Container, include the capabilities field in the securityContext section of the Container manifest.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set capabilities for a Container”

notes.front: What is base64, as used for Secret data?
notes.back: A way of encoding data as text. Anyone can decode it with `base64 --decode`; it is not encryption.
notes.explanation: kubectl stores the Secret values base64-encoded, and the task pages decode them with the base64 program.
notes.example: Like writing a note in capital letters instead of lower case: it looks different, but anyone can still read it.
notes.evidence: First, use a base64 encoding tool to convert your username and password to a base64 representation.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Convert your secret data to a base-64 representation”

notes.front: You run `kubectl create configmap` with three `--from-literal` pairs. How are they stored?
notes.back: Each pair becomes a separate entry in the ConfigMap's `data` section.
notes.explanation: You can pass as many key-value pairs on the command line as you need.
notes.evidence: You can pass in multiple key-value pairs. Each pair provided on the command line is represented as a separate entry in the data section of the ConfigMap.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Create a ConfigMap using kubectl create configmap”

notes.front: Which command creates a ConfigMap `app-cfg` with `mode=fast` and `level=3`, without writing a file?
notes.back: `kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=mode=fast --from-literal=level=3`
notes.choices:
A) kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=mode=fast --from-literal=level=3
B) kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=mode=fast,level=3
C) kubectl create secret generic app-cfg --from-literal=mode=fast --from-literal=level=3
notes.choicesExplained: B: each key-value pair takes its own --from-literal flag. C: this makes a Secret, not a ConfigMap.
notes.explanation: Repeat `--from-literal` once for each key-value pair.
notes.evidence: kubectl create configmap special-config --from-literal=special.how=very --from-literal=special.type=charm
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Create a ConfigMap using kubectl create configmap”

notes.front: What does `kubectl create configmap game-config --from-file=<directory>/` do with the files in that directory?
notes.back: Packages each file into the ConfigMap; each file becomes an entry in its `data` section.
notes.explanation: In the page's example, two properties files in the directory appear as two entries of the ConfigMap's data.
notes.evidence: The above command packages each file, in this case, game.properties and ui.properties in the configure-pod-container/configmap/ directory into the game-config ConfigMap.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Create a ConfigMap using kubectl create configmap”

notes.front: You have `nginx.conf` and `mime.types` in `./conf/`. Which command turns both into one ConfigMap `web-conf`?
notes.back: `kubectl create configmap web-conf --from-file=./conf/`
notes.choices:
A) kubectl create configmap web-conf --from-file=./conf/
B) kubectl create configmap web-conf --from-literal=./conf/
C) kubectl create configmap web-conf --from-env-file=./conf/
notes.choicesExplained: B: --from-literal takes key=value pairs, not a path. C: --from-env-file reads `VAR=VAL` lines from one env-file, not a directory of files.
notes.explanation: Pointing `--from-file` at a directory packages each file in it into the ConfigMap.
notes.evidence: kubectl create configmap game-config --from-file=configure-pod-container/configmap/
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Create a ConfigMap using kubectl create configmap”

notes.front: What format must each line of a file passed to `--from-env-file` follow?
notes.back: `VAR=VAL`. Comment lines and blank lines are ignored.
notes.explanation: Each variable in the env-file becomes its own key in the ConfigMap, and since v1.23 the flag can be given several times.
notes.evidence: Each line in an env file has to be in VAR=VAL format.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Create a ConfigMap using kubectl create configmap”

notes.front: Which field sets one container environment variable from one key of a ConfigMap?
notes.back: `env[].valueFrom.configMapKeyRef`, giving the ConfigMap's `name` and the `key`.
notes.explanation: The variable gets its own name in the Pod, independent of the key's name in the ConfigMap.
notes.evidence: env: - name: SPECIAL_LEVEL_KEY valueFrom: configMapKeyRef: name: a-config key: akey
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Define a container environment variable with data from a single ConfigMap”

notes.front: Your app reads `DB_HOST`. The value is under the key `host` in the ConfigMap `db-cfg`, which has ten other keys you do not want. What do you add to the container?
notes.back: An `env` entry named `DB_HOST` with `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef: {name: db-cfg, key: host}`.
notes.choices:
A) env with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef
B) envFrom with configMapRef db-cfg
C) A volume from db-cfg
notes.choicesExplained: B: envFrom imports every key, and they keep their own names, so there would be no DB_HOST. C: a volume gives files, not an environment variable.
notes.explanation: A key reference picks one key and lets you choose the variable's name.
notes.evidence: env: - name: SPECIAL_LEVEL_KEY valueFrom: configMapKeyRef: name: a-config key: akey
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Define a container environment variable with data from a single ConfigMap”

notes.front: With `envFrom` and a ConfigMap, what becomes the name of each environment variable?
notes.back: The key from the ConfigMap.
notes.explanation: envFrom sets all of the ConfigMap's key-value pairs as environment variables in one go.
notes.evidence: Use envFrom to define all of the ConfigMap's data as container environment variables. The key from the ConfigMap becomes the environment variable name in the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Configure all key-value pairs in a ConfigMap as container environment variables”

notes.front: The ConfigMap `feature-flags` holds twelve keys, all valid variable names, and the app expects each as an environment variable of the same name. What is the shortest way to wire them in?
notes.back: `envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: feature-flags}}]` on the container.
notes.choices:
A) envFrom with configMapRef
B) Twelve env entries with configMapKeyRef
C) Mount the ConfigMap at /etc/flags
notes.choicesExplained: B: this works but is longer; envFrom already uses each key as the name. C: a mount gives files, not environment variables.
notes.explanation: envFrom brings in all the ConfigMap's keys, each as a variable named after its key.
notes.evidence: When you use envFrom , all the key-value pairs in the referenced ConfigMap or Secret are set as environment variables for the container.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Define Environment Variables for a Container”

notes.front: With `envFrom`, a ConfigMap key such as `1badkey` is not a valid variable name. Does the Pod still start?
notes.back: Yes. The invalid key is skipped and recorded in the event log.
notes.explanation: The kubelet logs a warning event listing each skipped key.
notes.evidence: keys that are considered invalid will be skipped. The pod will be allowed to start, but the invalid names will be recorded in the event log
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Restrictions”

notes.front: When a ConfigMap is added under a Pod's `volumes` and mounted, what appears at the `mountPath`?
notes.back: One file for each key in the ConfigMap, named after the key.
notes.explanation: The ConfigMap data is added to the directory given as volumeMounts.mountPath.
notes.evidence: Add the ConfigMap name under the volumes section of the Pod specification. This adds the ConfigMap data to the directory specified as volumeMounts.mountPath
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Populate a Volume with data stored in a ConfigMap”

notes.front: An app reads its settings from files in `/etc/app/`. The settings are in the ConfigMap `app-settings`. Which two parts of the Pod spec do you write?
notes.back: A volume with `configMap: {name: app-settings}`, and a `volumeMounts` entry with `mountPath: /etc/app`.
notes.choices:
A) volumes with configMap, plus volumeMounts with mountPath
B) envFrom with configMapRef
C) An emptyDir volume, then copy the ConfigMap in
notes.choicesExplained: B: envFrom makes environment variables, not files. C: an emptyDir starts empty; the configMap volume type fills the directory for you.
notes.explanation: The ConfigMap named under volumes is written to the directory given as the mount path.
notes.evidence: Add the ConfigMap name under the volumes section of the Pod specification. This adds the ConfigMap data to the directory specified as volumeMounts.mountPath
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Populate a Volume with data stored in a ConfigMap”

notes.front: In a ConfigMap volume, which field puts a chosen key at a chosen file path?
notes.back: `path`, in the volume's `items` list.
notes.explanation: As with a full mount, the files that were in the mount directory before become inaccessible.
notes.evidence: Use the path field to specify the desired file path for specific ConfigMap items.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Add ConfigMap data to a specific path in the Volume”

notes.front: You update a ConfigMap that a running Pod mounts as a volume. Does the Pod see the change?
notes.back: Yes, eventually: the projected files are updated, after up to the kubelet sync period plus its cache time-to-live.
notes.explanation: Both default to one minute, and updating one of the Pod's annotations triggers an immediate refresh.
notes.evidence: When a mounted ConfigMap is updated, the projected content is eventually updated too.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Mounted ConfigMaps are updated automatically”

notes.front: Unlike a mounted ConfigMap, what happens to environment variables taken from a ConfigMap when it changes?
notes.back: Nothing: they are not updated automatically. The Pod must be restarted.
notes.explanation: A container that mounts the ConfigMap with subPath does not receive updates either.
notes.evidence: ConfigMaps consumed as environment variables are not updated automatically and require a pod restart. Note: A container using a ConfigMap as a subPath volume mount will not receive ConfigMap updates.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “ConfigMaps”, “Mounted ConfigMaps are updated automatically”

notes.front: You change `LOG_LEVEL` in a ConfigMap. Container `app` reads it through `envFrom`; container `web` reads a file from a full ConfigMap volume; container `job` mounts the same file with `subPath`. Which picks up the new value without a restart?
notes.back: Only `web`, the container that mounts the whole ConfigMap as a volume.
notes.choices:
A) Only web
B) app and web
C) web and job
D) All three
notes.choicesExplained: B: `app` reads environment variables, which are not updated without a restart. C, D: `job` uses a subPath mount, which does not receive ConfigMap updates.
notes.explanation: Only a full ConfigMap volume is refreshed by the kubelet.
notes.evidence: ConfigMaps consumed as environment variables are not updated automatically and require a pod restart. Note: A container using a ConfigMap as a subPath volume mount will not receive ConfigMap updates.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “ConfigMaps”, “Mounted ConfigMaps are updated automatically”

notes.front: A Pod references a ConfigMap that does not exist, and the reference is not marked optional. What happens?
notes.back: The Pod won't start.
notes.explanation: You must create the ConfigMap before you reference it, or mark the reference optional.
notes.evidence: You must create the ConfigMap object before you reference it in a Pod specification. Alternatively, mark the ConfigMap reference as optional in the Pod spec (see Optional ConfigMaps). If you reference a ConfigMap that doesn't exist and you don't mark the reference as optional , the Pod won't start.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Restrictions”

notes.front: Can a Pod in namespace `web` use a ConfigMap from namespace `shared`?
notes.back: No. Pods can only refer to ConfigMaps in their own namespace.
notes.explanation: ConfigMaps live in a specific namespace; static Pods cannot use ConfigMaps at all.
notes.evidence: Pods can only refer to ConfigMaps that are in the same namespace as the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Restrictions”

notes.front: A Deployment in `prod` mounts the ConfigMap `app-cfg`, which exists only in `staging`. The reference is not optional. What happens, and what is the fix?
notes.back: Its Pods won't start. Create `app-cfg` in `prod`.
notes.choices:
A) Pods won't start; create the ConfigMap in prod
B) Pods start and read the staging copy
C) Pods start with an empty directory
notes.choicesExplained: B: a Pod can only use ConfigMaps in its own namespace. C: an empty mount happens only when the reference is marked optional.
notes.explanation: For this Pod the ConfigMap does not exist, and a missing non-optional reference stops the Pod starting.
notes.evidence: If you reference a ConfigMap that doesn't exist and you don't mark the reference as optional , the Pod won't start.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Restrictions”

notes.front: A ConfigMap volume is marked `optional: true` and the ConfigMap does not exist. What does the container see at the mount path?
notes.back: An empty directory: the mount path is still created, and the Pod starts.
notes.explanation: If the ConfigMap exists but a referenced key does not, that key's path is simply absent.
notes.evidence: If the ConfigMap is non-existent, the mounted volume will be empty. If the ConfigMap exists, but the referenced key is non-existent, the path will be absent beneath the mount point.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap”, “Optional ConfigMaps”

notes.front: Once a ConfigMap has `immutable: true`, how can you change its data?
notes.back: You cannot. You can only delete and recreate the ConfigMap; the flag cannot be reverted either.
notes.explanation: Marking it immutable also lets the kube-apiserver close its watches on it, reducing load.
notes.evidence: Once a ConfigMap is marked as immutable, it is not possible to revert this change nor to mutate the contents of the data or the binaryData field. You can only delete and recreate the ConfigMap.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “ConfigMaps”, “Immutable ConfigMaps”

notes.front: What is the difference between `env` and `envFrom` on a container?
notes.back: `env` names each variable and gives its value directly. `envFrom` sets every key of a referenced ConfigMap or Secret as a variable.
notes.explanation: With envFrom you can also give a common prefix for the imported names.
notes.evidence: allows you to set environment variables for a container, specifying a value directly for each variable that you name. envFrom : allows you to set environment variables for a container by referencing either a ConfigMap or a Secret.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Define Environment Variables for a Container”, “Define an environment variable for a container”

notes.front: A container needs `REGION=eu-west` and nothing else, and no ConfigMap exists for it. What do you add?
notes.back: `env: [{name: REGION, value: eu-west}]` on the container.
notes.choices:
A) env with name and value
B) envFrom with the value eu-west
C) An annotation `REGION=eu-west`
notes.choicesExplained: B: envFrom references a ConfigMap or Secret; it cannot hold a value itself. C: annotations are metadata, not environment variables.
notes.explanation: env sets a value directly for each variable you name.
notes.evidence: To set environment variables, include the env or envFrom field in the configuration file.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Define Environment Variables for a Container”, “Define an environment variable for a container”

notes.front: `GREETING` and `NAME` are defined in a container's `env`. How can `args` use them?
notes.back: As `$(GREETING)` and `$(NAME)`.
notes.explanation: Variables defined under env can be used elsewhere in the configuration, such as in commands and arguments.
notes.evidence: Environment variables that you define in a Pod's configuration under .spec.containers[*].env[*] can be used elsewhere in the configuration, for example in commands and arguments that you set for the Pod's containers.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Define Environment Variables for a Container”, “Using environment variables inside of your config”

notes.front: In `kubectl create secret generic --from-literal=password=...`, how should you write a value containing `$`, `!` or `*`?
notes.back: Inside single quotes, so the shell does not interpret those characters.
notes.explanation: Without single quotes, your shell would treat the special characters itself before kubectl saw them.
notes.evidence: You must use single quotes '' to escape special characters such as $ , \ , * , = , and ! in your strings. If you don't, your shell will interpret these characters.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Secrets using kubectl”, “Use raw data”

notes.front: Which command creates a Secret `db-cred` with `user=app` and `pass=p@$$!`?
notes.back: `kubectl create secret generic db-cred --from-literal=user=app --from-literal=pass='p@$$!'`
notes.choices:
A) kubectl create secret generic db-cred --from-literal=user=app --from-literal=pass='p@$$!'
B) kubectl create secret db-cred --from-literal=user=app --from-literal=pass=p@$$!
C) kubectl create configmap db-cred --from-literal=user=app --from-literal=pass='p@$$!'
notes.choicesExplained: B: it lacks the generic subcommand, and the unquoted $ and ! would be changed by the shell. C: this makes a ConfigMap, which is not meant for confidential data.
notes.explanation: `secret generic` makes an Opaque Secret, and single quotes protect the special characters.
notes.evidence: kubectl create secret generic db-user-pass \ --from-literal=username=admin \ --from-literal=password='S!B\*d$zDsb='
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Secrets using kubectl”, “Use raw data”

notes.front: With `kubectl create secret generic --from-file=./password.txt`, what is the key called, and how do you choose another?
notes.back: The key is the file name, `password.txt`. Use `--from-file=<key>=<source>` to choose it.
notes.explanation: The key name is optional; without it the file's name is used.
notes.evidence: The default key name is the file name. You can optionally set the key name using --from-file=[key=]source .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Secrets using kubectl”, “Use source files”

notes.front: The app expects a Secret key named `token`, but the value is in `./api-token.txt`. Which command?
notes.back: `kubectl create secret generic api --from-file=token=./api-token.txt`
notes.choices:
A) kubectl create secret generic api --from-file=token=./api-token.txt
B) kubectl create secret generic api --from-file=./api-token.txt
C) kubectl create secret generic api --from-literal=token=./api-token.txt
notes.choicesExplained: B: the key would be api-token.txt, the file name. C: the value would be the literal text ./api-token.txt, not the file's contents.
notes.explanation: `key=source` sets the key name; the value is read from the file.
notes.evidence: The default key name is the file name. You can optionally set the key name using --from-file=[key=]source .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Secrets using kubectl”, “Use source files”

notes.front: Why does the Secrets task write its files with `echo -n`?
notes.back: So the files have no extra newline at the end; otherwise the newline is encoded into the Secret too.
notes.explanation: kubectl encodes the whole file content into base64, newline included.
notes.evidence: The -n flag ensures that the generated files do not have an extra newline character at the end of the text. This is important because when kubectl reads a file and encodes the content into a base64 string, the extra newline character gets encoded too.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Secrets using kubectl”, “Use source files”

notes.front: How do you read the plain value of the key `password` in the Secret `db-user-pass` in one command?
notes.back: `kubectl get secret db-user-pass -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode`
notes.explanation: The page recommends combining view and decode, rather than pasting the encoded value into a separate command that shell history would keep.
notes.evidence: A better approach is to combine the view and decode commands.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Secrets using kubectl”, “Decoding the Secret”

notes.front: `kubectl get secret api -o jsonpath='{.data.token}'` prints `c2VjcmV0`. What does it hold, and what do you run next to read it?
notes.back: The base64-encoded value. Pipe it through `base64 --decode`.
notes.choices:
A) Base64-encoded; pipe to base64 --decode
B) Encrypted; you need the cluster's encryption key
C) A hash; the value cannot be recovered
notes.choicesExplained: B: the data is only encoded, and by default is stored unencrypted. C: base64 is reversible by anyone.
notes.explanation: Secret data is shown base64-encoded, and the base64 program decodes it.
notes.evidence: kubectl get secret db-user-pass -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Secrets using kubectl”, “Decoding the Secret”

notes.front: How are Kubernetes Secrets stored by default, and who can read or change them?
notes.back: Unencrypted in the API server's data store (etcd). Anyone with API access, or access to etcd, can retrieve or modify them.
notes.explanation: The page's first safety step is to enable encryption at rest for Secrets, then least-privilege access rules.
notes.evidence: Kubernetes Secrets are, by default, stored unencrypted in the API server's underlying data store (etcd). Anyone with API access can retrieve or modify a Secret, and so can anyone with access to etcd.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”

notes.front: A developer may not read Secrets in `payments`, but may create Deployments there. Can they get at the Secrets?
notes.back: Yes. Anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace, even indirectly through a Deployment, can use that to read any Secret in it.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, through a Pod that mounts them
B) No: reading Secrets needs its own permission
C) Only if Secrets are base64-encoded
notes.choicesExplained: B: the page warns that Pod creation rights give indirect access to Secrets. C: Secret data is always base64-encoded; that is not a protection.
notes.explanation: The page counts the ability to create a Deployment as indirect access to the namespace's Secrets.
notes.evidence: anyone who is authorized to create a Pod in a namespace can use that access to read any Secret in that namespace; this includes indirect access such as the ability to create a Deployment.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”

notes.front: Which Secret type holds arbitrary user-defined data, and is the default when no type is given?
notes.back: `Opaque`. kubectl makes one with `create secret generic`.
notes.explanation: An empty type string is also treated as Opaque.
notes.evidence: Opaque is the default Secret type if you don't explicitly specify a type in a Secret manifest. When you create a Secret using kubectl , you must use the generic subcommand to indicate an Opaque Secret type.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Opaque Secrets”

notes.front: The built-in Secret type for a ServiceAccount token is {{c1::kubernetes.io/service-account-token}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the built-in types Kubernetes provides for common uses.
notes.evidence: Opaque arbitrary user-defined data kubernetes.io/service-account-token ServiceAccount token
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: The built-in Secret type for a serialised legacy `~/.dockercfg` file is {{c1::kubernetes.io/dockercfg}}.
notes.explanation: It has a sibling for the newer `~/.docker/config.json` format.
notes.evidence: kubernetes.io/dockercfg serialized ~/.dockercfg file kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson serialized ~/.docker/config.json file
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: The built-in Secret type for a serialised `~/.docker/config.json` file is {{c1::kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson}}.
notes.explanation: `kubectl create secret docker-registry` produces this type, used for pulling images from a private registry.
notes.evidence: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson serialized ~/.docker/config.json file
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: The built-in Secret type for credentials for basic authentication is {{c1::kubernetes.io/basic-auth}}.
notes.explanation: The type tells Kubernetes which validations and constraints to apply to the Secret's data.
notes.evidence: kubernetes.io/basic-auth credentials for basic authentication
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: The built-in Secret type for `SSH` authentication credentials is {{c1::kubernetes.io/ssh-auth}}.
notes.explanation: Built-in types vary in the validations performed and the constraints Kubernetes imposes.
notes.evidence: kubernetes.io/ssh-auth credentials for SSH authentication
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: The built-in Secret type for data for a TLS client or server is {{c1::kubernetes.io/tls}}.
notes.explanation: `kubectl create secret tls` produces this type from a certificate and key.
notes.evidence: kubernetes.io/tls data for a TLS client or server
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: The built-in Secret type for bootstrap token data is {{c1::bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token}}.
notes.explanation: Its name starts with `bootstrap.kubernetes.io/`, while the other prefixed types in the table start with `kubernetes.io/`.
notes.evidence: bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token bootstrap token data
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: You need a Secret holding a certificate and private key for a web server, and another holding login details for a private image registry. Which types?
notes.back: `kubernetes.io/tls` for the certificate; `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` for the registry login.
notes.choices:
A) kubernetes.io/tls and kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
B) Opaque and kubernetes.io/basic-auth
C) kubernetes.io/ssh-auth and kubernetes.io/service-account-token
notes.choicesExplained: B: Opaque would work but loses the type's validation, and basic-auth is not the registry config format. C: ssh-auth is for `SSH` credentials and service-account-token for ServiceAccounts.
notes.explanation: Each built-in type is meant for one usage scenario.
notes.evidence: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson serialized ~/.docker/config.json file kubernetes.io/basic-auth credentials for basic authentication kubernetes.io/ssh-auth credentials for SSH authentication kubernetes.io/tls data for a TLS client or server
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Types of Secret”

notes.front: Which kubectl command creates a TLS Secret, and what must already exist?
notes.back: `kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=<cert file> --key=<key file>`. The public/private key pair must exist beforehand.
notes.explanation: The certificate given to --cert must match the private key given to --key.
notes.evidence: To create a TLS Secret using kubectl , use the tls subcommand: kubectl create secret tls my-tls-secret \ --cert = path/to/cert/file \ --key = path/to/key/file The public/private key pair must exist before hand.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “TLS Secrets”

notes.front: A Pod mounts a Secret volume at `/etc/foo` with `defaultMode: 0400`. What does the container find there?
notes.back: One file per Secret key under `/etc/foo`, each with permission 0400.
notes.explanation: defaultMode sets the permission of every file the Secret volume creates.
notes.evidence: The Secret is mounted on /etc/foo ; all the files created by the secret volume mount have permission 0400 .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Set POSIX permissions for Secret keys”

notes.front: An app reads its certificate from files in `/certs`, and only the owner may read them. The data is in the Secret `web-tls`. What do you write in the Pod spec?
notes.back: A volume `secret: {secretName: web-tls, defaultMode: 0400}` and a volumeMount at `/certs`.
notes.choices:
A) A secret volume with secretName and defaultMode 0400, mounted at /certs
B) envFrom with secretRef web-tls
C) A configMap volume named web-tls
notes.choicesExplained: B: envFrom gives environment variables, not files. C: a configMap volume reads a ConfigMap, not a Secret.
notes.explanation: A secret volume writes each key as a file, and defaultMode sets the permissions.
notes.evidence: volumes: - name: foo secret: secretName: mysecret defaultMode: 0400
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Set POSIX permissions for Secret keys”

notes.front: In a Pod written in JSON rather than YAML, how must you give `defaultMode` 0400?
notes.back: As a decimal value (256), because JSON reads 0400 as decimal 400.
notes.explanation: YAML accepts the octal form; the JSON specification does not support octal literals.
notes.evidence: beware that the JSON specification doesn't support octal literals for numbers because JSON considers 0400 to be the decimal value 400 . In JSON, use decimal values for the defaultMode instead.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Set POSIX permissions for Secret keys”

notes.front: Which field sets one container environment variable from one key of a Secret?
notes.back: `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef`.
notes.explanation: You add one such variable for each Secret key you want, and the program reads the value from that variable.
notes.evidence: add an environment variable for each Secret key that you want to use to the env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef field.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Using Secrets as environment variables”

notes.front: The app needs `DB_PASSWORD` from the key `password` of the Secret `db-cred`. What do you add to the container?
notes.back: An `env` entry `DB_PASSWORD` with `valueFrom.secretKeyRef: {name: db-cred, key: password}`.
notes.choices:
A) env with valueFrom.secretKeyRef
B) env with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef
C) envFrom with secretRef db-cred
notes.choicesExplained: B: configMapKeyRef reads a ConfigMap, not a Secret. C: envFrom would name the variable password, not DB_PASSWORD.
notes.explanation: A key reference takes one Secret key and lets you name the variable.
notes.evidence: Assign the backend-username value defined in the Secret to the SECRET_USERNAME environment variable in the Pod specification.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Define a container environment variable with data from a single Secret”

notes.front: With `envFrom` and a Secret, what becomes the name of each environment variable?
notes.back: The key from the Secret.
notes.explanation: envFrom defines all of the Secret's data as container environment variables at once.
notes.evidence: Use envFrom to define all of the Secret's data as container environment variables. The key from the Secret becomes the environment variable name in the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Configure all key-value pairs in a Secret as container environment variables”

notes.front: The Secret `smtp` has keys `SMTP_USER` and `SMTP_PASS`, exactly the variable names the app expects. What is the shortest container setting?
notes.back: `envFrom: [{secretRef: {name: smtp}}]`
notes.choices:
A) envFrom with secretRef smtp
B) envFrom with configMapRef smtp
C) A secret volume named smtp
notes.choicesExplained: B: configMapRef reads a ConfigMap. C: a volume gives files, not environment variables.
notes.explanation: Each key becomes a variable of the same name.
notes.evidence: Use envFrom to define all of the Secret's data as container environment variables. The key from the Secret becomes the environment variable name in the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Configure all key-value pairs in a Secret as container environment variables”

notes.front: A container reads a Secret through an environment variable, and the Secret is updated. When does the container see the new value?
notes.back: Only after it is restarted.
notes.explanation: The page notes third-party tools exist to trigger restarts when Secrets change.
notes.evidence: If a container already consumes a Secret in an environment variable, a Secret update will not be seen by the container unless it is restarted.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Distribute Credentials Securely Using Secrets”, “Define container environment variables using Secret data”

notes.front: An existing Secret is changed to `immutable: true`. What can you do if its data later needs to change?
notes.back: Only delete and recreate it; the change cannot be reverted and the data cannot be edited.
notes.explanation: Existing Pods keep a mount point to the deleted Secret, so the page recommends recreating those Pods.
notes.evidence: Once a Secret or ConfigMap is marked as immutable, it is not possible to revert this change nor to mutate the contents of the data field. You can only delete and recreate the Secret.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Secrets”, “Immutable Secrets”

notes.front: What ServiceAccount does every namespace have?
notes.back: At least one: the ServiceAccount called `default`.
notes.explanation: You can list the namespace's ServiceAccounts with `kubectl get serviceaccounts`.
notes.evidence: Every namespace has at least one ServiceAccount: the default ServiceAccount resource, called default .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Use more than one ServiceAccount”

notes.front: You create a Pod without `spec.serviceAccountName`. What does `kubectl get pod -o yaml` show?
notes.back: A `spec.serviceAccountName` anyway: Kubernetes sets it automatically.
notes.explanation: The Pod then runs as that ServiceAccount, and an app in it can reach the API with automatically mounted credentials.
notes.evidence: In the output, you see a field spec.serviceAccountName . Kubernetes automatically sets that value if you don't specify it when you create a Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Use the default service account to access the API server”

notes.front: A Pod in namespace `batch` was created with no ServiceAccount set. Which identity does it use to call the API?
notes.back: The `default` ServiceAccount of the `batch` namespace.
notes.choices:
A) The default ServiceAccount of batch
B) No identity: it cannot reach the API
C) The user who created the Pod
notes.choicesExplained: B: the field is filled in automatically and credentials are mounted automatically. C: a Pod authenticates as a ServiceAccount, not as its creator.
notes.explanation: Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount, and Kubernetes sets serviceAccountName when you leave it out.
notes.evidence: Every namespace has at least one ServiceAccount: the default ServiceAccount resource, called default .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Use more than one ServiceAccount”

notes.front: What must the name of a new ServiceAccount be?
notes.back: A valid DNS subdomain name.
notes.explanation: You create extra ServiceAccounts like any other object, for example by applying a small ServiceAccount manifest.
notes.evidence: The name of a ServiceAccount object must be a valid DNS subdomain name.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Use more than one ServiceAccount”

notes.front: You have created the ServiceAccount `build-robot`. How does a Pod run as it?
notes.back: Set `spec.serviceAccountName: build-robot` in the Pod.
notes.choices:
A) spec.serviceAccountName: build-robot
B) metadata.labels: serviceaccount=build-robot
C) A RoleBinding naming the Pod
notes.choicesExplained: B: labels do not choose an identity. C: a RoleBinding grants permissions to a ServiceAccount; it does not assign one to a Pod.
notes.explanation: The Pod's spec names the ServiceAccount it runs as.
notes.evidence: kind: Pod metadata: name: my-pod spec: serviceAccountName: build-robot
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Opt out of API credential automounting”

notes.front: Where can you set `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, and which wins if both disagree?
notes.back: On the ServiceAccount or on the Pod's spec. The Pod spec takes precedence.
notes.explanation: Setting it on the Pod opts that one Pod out; on the ServiceAccount, it opts out Pods using it.
notes.evidence: If both the ServiceAccount and the Pod's .spec specify a value for automountServiceAccountToken , the Pod spec takes precedence.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Opt out of API credential automounting”

notes.front: The ServiceAccount `web` has `automountServiceAccountToken: false`. One Pod using it sets `automountServiceAccountToken: true`. Is the token mounted in that Pod?
notes.back: Yes. The Pod spec takes precedence over the ServiceAccount.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the Pod spec wins
B) No, the ServiceAccount wins
C) The Pod is rejected for the conflict
notes.choicesExplained: B: the ServiceAccount's value applies only when the Pod does not set one. C: disagreement is allowed; one value simply takes precedence.
notes.explanation: When both specify a value, the Pod spec's value is used.
notes.evidence: If both the ServiceAccount and the Pod's .spec specify a value for automountServiceAccountToken , the Pod spec takes precedence.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Opt out of API credential automounting”

notes.front: What does `kubectl create token build-robot` give you, and how do you ask for a particular lifetime?
notes.back: A time-limited token to authenticate as that ServiceAccount. Use `--duration`; the issued lifetime may differ.
notes.explanation: The actual duration of the issued token might be shorter, or even longer, than requested.
notes.evidence: You can get a time-limited API token for that ServiceAccount using kubectl
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Manually create an API token for a ServiceAccount”

notes.front: A CI job outside the cluster needs a short-lived token for the ServiceAccount `deployer`. Which command?
notes.back: `kubectl create token deployer` (add `--duration` to request a lifetime).
notes.choices:
A) kubectl create token deployer
B) kubectl get secret deployer -o yaml
C) kubectl create serviceaccount deployer --token
notes.choicesExplained: B: ServiceAccounts do not come with a token Secret to read unless one was created. C: creating the account does not issue a token.
notes.explanation: create token issues a time-limited token for an existing ServiceAccount.
notes.evidence: You can request a specific token duration using the --duration command line argument to kubectl create token (the actual duration of the issued token might be shorter, or could even be longer).
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Manually create an API token for a ServiceAccount”

notes.front: How do you get a ServiceAccount token stored in a Secret, for example one that never expires?
notes.back: Create a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` with the annotation `kubernetes.io/service-account.name: <account>`.
notes.explanation: Because of the annotation, the control plane fills the Secret with a token for that ServiceAccount.
notes.evidence: If you want to obtain an API token for a ServiceAccount, you create a new Secret with a special annotation, kubernetes.io/service-account.name .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Manually create an API token for a ServiceAccount”

notes.front: What limits the life of the ServiceAccount tokens mounted into Pods through a projected volume?
notes.back: They have bounded lifetimes and are invalidated automatically when the Pod is deleted.
notes.explanation: They are obtained through the TokenRequest API; a manually created token Secret is still possible if you need one that never expires.
notes.evidence: The tokens obtained using this method have bounded lifetimes, and are automatically invalidated when the Pod they are mounted into is deleted.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”

notes.front: How can every Pod in a namespace pull from a private registry without listing `imagePullSecrets` itself?
notes.back: Add the registry Secret to the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount as an imagePullSecret.
notes.explanation: The task does it with `kubectl patch serviceaccount default` and then shows the Secret in a new Pod's spec.
notes.evidence: Next, modify the default service account for the namespace to use this Secret as an imagePullSecret.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure Service Accounts for Pods”, “Add ImagePullSecrets to a service account”

notes.front: Security settings in a Pod's `spec.securityContext` apply to which containers?
notes.back: All the containers in the Pod.
notes.explanation: The Pod-level field is a PodSecurityContext object, holding settings such as runAsUser, runAsGroup and fsGroup.
notes.evidence: The securityContext field is a PodSecurityContext object. The security settings that you specify for a Pod apply to all Containers in the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the security context for a Pod”

notes.front: A Pod sets `runAsUser: 1000` and `runAsGroup: 3000`. What user and primary group do its processes run with, and what if runAsGroup is left out?
notes.back: User 1000 and group 3000. Without runAsGroup, the primary group is root (0).
notes.explanation: Files the processes create are also owned by user 1000 and group 3000.
notes.evidence: The runAsGroup field specifies the primary group ID of 3000 for all processes within any containers of the Pod. If this field is omitted, the primary group ID of the containers will be root(0).
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the security context for a Pod”

notes.front: Both containers in a Pod must run as user 1000 and group 3000. Where is the least repetitive place to set this?
notes.back: Once, in the Pod's `spec.securityContext` (`runAsUser: 1000`, `runAsGroup: 3000`).
notes.choices:
A) In spec.securityContext
B) In each container's image only
C) In an annotation on the Pod
notes.choicesExplained: B: the image can set a user, but the task is to set it in the Pod. C: annotations do not set process identity.
notes.explanation: Pod-level settings apply to all containers in the Pod.
notes.evidence: The security settings that you specify for a Pod apply to all Containers in the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the security context for a Pod”

notes.front: A Pod sets `fsGroup: 2000` and mounts a volume at `/data/demo`. What does fsGroup do?
notes.back: Adds 2000 as a supplementary group of the container processes, and makes group 2000 own the volume and new files in it.
notes.explanation: So the volume's files belong to a group that every process in the Pod is also a member of.
notes.evidence: Since fsGroup field is specified, all processes of the container are also part of the supplementary group ID 2000. The owner for volume /data/demo and any files created in that volume will be Group ID 2000.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the security context for a Pod”

notes.front: A container runs as user 1000, but cannot write to a mounted persistent volume owned by root. Which Pod-level field gives its processes a group that owns the volume?
notes.back: `fsGroup` in the Pod's `securityContext`.
notes.choices:
A) fsGroup
B) runAsGroup
C) readOnlyRootFilesystem
notes.choicesExplained: B: runAsGroup sets the processes' primary group; it does not change the volume's owner. C: this makes the root filesystem read-only, the opposite of what is needed.
notes.explanation: fsGroup makes that group the owner of the volume and adds it to the processes' groups.
notes.evidence: The owner for volume /data/demo and any files created in that volume will be Group ID 2000.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the security context for a Pod”

notes.front: A Pod and one of its containers both set a security setting, with different values. Which applies to that container?
notes.back: The container's value: container settings override the Pod's where they overlap.
notes.explanation: Container settings apply only to that container and do not affect the Pod's volumes.
notes.evidence: Security settings that you specify for a Container apply only to the individual Container, and they override settings made at the Pod level when there is overlap. Container settings do not affect the Pod's Volumes.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the security context for a Container”

notes.front: A Pod sets `runAsUser: 1000`. Its container `api` sets `runAsUser: 2000`; its container `sidecar` sets nothing. Which user does each run as?
notes.back: `api` runs as 2000; `sidecar` runs as 1000.
notes.choices:
A) api 2000, sidecar 1000
B) Both 1000
C) Both 2000
notes.choicesExplained: B: the container setting overrides the Pod's for api. C: a container setting applies only to its own container.
notes.explanation: Where settings overlap, the container level wins, and only for that container.
notes.evidence: Security settings that you specify for a Container apply only to the individual Container, and they override settings made at the Pod level when there is overlap.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the security context for a Container”

notes.front: Where do you add or drop Linux capabilities, and how do you write `CAP_SYS_TIME` there?
notes.back: In the `capabilities` field of the container's `securityContext`, without the `CAP_` part: `SYS_TIME`.
notes.explanation: Linux capability constants have the form `CAP_XXX`, but the manifest omits the prefix.
notes.evidence: Linux capability constants have the form CAP_XXX . But when you list capabilities in your container manifest, you must omit the CAP_ portion of the constant.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set capabilities for a Container”

notes.front: A network tool in a container needs `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, and nothing else in the Pod should get it. What do you write?
notes.back: In that container's `securityContext`: `capabilities: {add: ["NET_ADMIN"]}`.
notes.choices:
A) Container securityContext, capabilities add NET_ADMIN
B) Pod securityContext, capabilities add CAP_NET_ADMIN
C) privileged: true on the Pod
notes.choicesExplained: B: capabilities are set per container, and the manifest omits the CAP_ prefix. C: privileged grants far more than one capability.
notes.explanation: Capabilities go in the container's securityContext, listed without CAP_.
notes.evidence: To add or drop Linux capabilities for a Container, include the capabilities field in the securityContext section of the Container manifest.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set capabilities for a Container”

notes.front: What does `allowPrivilegeEscalation` control, and what is its value if you leave it out?
notes.back: Whether a process can gain more privileges than its parent, for example through a setuid binary. It defaults to true.
notes.explanation: It works through the kernel's `no_new_privs` flag, which is set when `allowPrivilegeEscalation` is false.
notes.evidence: Controls whether a process can gain more privileges than its parent process, for example, by executing a setuid binary.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”

notes.front: A container sets `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` and also adds the capability `SYS_ADMIN`. What is wrong?
notes.back: The combination is inconsistent: allowPrivilegeEscalation false cannot be set with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` (or with privileged).
notes.choices:
A) The two settings cannot be combined
B) Nothing; they are independent
C) SYS_ADMIN must be written CAP_SYS_ADMIN
notes.choicesExplained: B: the page says the two are inconsistent. C: the manifest omits the CAP_ prefix, so SYS_ADMIN is the right spelling.
notes.explanation: Turning off escalation contradicts running privileged or holding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`.
notes.evidence: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false is inconsistent, and therefore cannot be set in combination, with a container that: - is run as privileged, or - has the capability CAP_SYS_ADMIN
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”

notes.front: The securityContext field that mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only is {{c1::readOnlyRootFilesystem}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the container security settings the page lists, alongside allowPrivilegeEscalation and capabilities.
notes.evidence: readOnlyRootFilesystem : Mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”

notes.front: A hardening rule says the app must not be able to change any file in its image. Which container setting enforces this?
notes.back: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` in the container's `securityContext`.
notes.choices:
A) readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
B) allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
C) runAsGroup: 0
notes.choicesExplained: B: this stops gaining privileges, not writing files. C: group 0 is root's group, which does not make anything read-only.
notes.explanation: This setting mounts the root filesystem read-only.
notes.evidence: readOnlyRootFilesystem : Mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”

notes.front: What are the valid `seccompProfile.type` values, and which uses the container runtime's default profile?
notes.back: `RuntimeDefault`, `Unconfined` and `Localhost`. `RuntimeDefault` uses the runtime's default profile.
notes.explanation: `localhostProfile` may be set only with `type: Localhost`, pointing to a profile file on the node.
notes.evidence: Valid options for type include RuntimeDefault , Unconfined , and Localhost . localhostProfile must only be set if type: Localhost .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container”, “Set the Seccomp Profile for a Container”
